name: Philips Lumea

lead: The Philips Lumea is a handheld consumer device that uses intense pulsed light (IPL) for long-term hair reduction at home, on the body and face, as an alternative to clinic treatment. The payoff is smoother, less hairy skin.

IPL flashes broad-spectrum light that is absorbed by melanin in the hair, heating and damaging the follicle. Only hairs in the growth phase respond, so treatments are repeated over weeks. Clinical IPL generally reduces hair growth and is described as typically less effective than laser; evidence for this specific model is limited.

paras: Users flash the device over shaved skin in repeated sessions over weeks, then do occasional maintenance. It suits darker hair on lighter skin; light, grey, red and white hair respond poorly.
Reported risks of IPL include hyperpigmentation and eye injury if misused; a review of home IPL safety discussed the need for eye safety in consumer designs.

angle.text: The Philips Lumea is used at home for long-term hair reduction on the body and face. Pulsed light heats the follicles, so hair growth slows over sessions and skin looks smoother. Home IPL has some trial support for hair reduction; evidence for this model is limited.

lead: The Philips Lumea is a handheld consumer device that uses intense pulsed light (IPL) for hair removal at home. People use it to reduce hair on the legs, underarms, bikini line and other areas over a series of sessions, so the skin looks smoother with less shaving or waxing. Philips markets it as a lower-cost alternative to salon laser treatment.[1]

IPL is not a laser: a xenon flashlamp emits broad-spectrum light of roughly 400 to 1200 nm that is absorbed mainly by melanin in the hair, heating the follicle.[2][3] Philips describes the pulses as sending hair into a resting phase so it falls out, and reports results from its own studies, such as a 92 percent reduction on the lower legs after 12 treatments.[1] Wikipedia's IPL article describes IPL as less effective than laser hair removal while noting many patients are satisfied.[3]

In December 2025 the US FDA cleared a Lumea IPL under a Special 510(k) as an over-the-counter device indicated for hair removal and for permanent reduction in hair regrowth.[2] No independent published trial of the Lumea is known; the studies Philips cites are its own.
infobox: Home intense pulsed light (IPL) hair-removal device
Cleared, Special 510(k) K253754, 23 Dec 2025; Class 2, over-the-counter[2]
Ages 18 to 65, fair to medium brown skin, dark blond to black hair[2]
Monthly touch-ups advised by the maker[1]

paras: IPL devices emit light filtered to roughly 400 to 1200 nm; melanin in the hair absorbs it and the heat damages the follicle.[3] Only hairs in the active growth phase respond to a given session, so clinical IPL usually takes around 8 to 10 treatments spaced 4 to 6 weeks apart.[3] IPL reduces the number of hairs but does not remove all hair.[3]

Philips describes Lumea as an at-home version of salon-derived IPL that sends hair into a resting phase so it falls out, and says consistent use keeps skin hair-free. Its pages report over 80 percent reduction after two treatments in lab-style measurements, and up to five years of smooth-feeling skin on higher-end series and three years on the 7000 series with monthly touch-ups.[1]

Philips says IPL works on hair from dark blonde through black and on skin from fair to brown, and offers an online test to check suitability.[1] The FDA-cleared labeling limits users to ages 18 to 65 with fair to medium brown skin and naturally dark blond, brown, dark brown or black hair.[2] Wikipedia notes that photosensitizing medications and existing skin damage are contraindications and that one manufacturer restricts IPL and laser devices to light to medium skin tones.[3]

The FDA record for K253754 lists Philips Consumer Lifestyle B.V. as applicant, a decision of substantial equivalence on 23 December 2025, a xenon arc flashlamp, Class 2 classification under 21 CFR 878.4810 and over-the-counter home use. It names an earlier Lumea IPL clearance, K243453, as its predicate.[2] Philips states the line also holds EU MDR clearance.[1]

No studies found on the Lumea in independent peer-reviewed publications. Philips reports in-house results, including a median 86 percent reduction on the lower legs 18 months after the third treatment and a test population of more than 3,000 women.[1] Studies of IPL as a category report significant hair reduction, with side effects compared in one 2006 comparison at 15.3 percent for IPL against 28.9 percent for diode lasers and 9.5 percent for alexandrite lasers, all temporary.[3]

The main complication described for IPL is hyperpigmentation, and side effects in the comparison above were temporary.[3] Philips says Lumea does not treat white, grey, light blonde or red hair and is unsuitable for very dark skin.[1][2]
Home IPL is used as a way to reduce body and facial hair, appealing to people who want long-lasting smoothness without repeated clinic visits.

timeline.event: Philips Consumer Lifestyle B.V. receives FDA 510(k) clearance for a Lumea IPL (K253754) on 23 December, referencing the earlier K243453.[2]
